blocks.content: 1. What is DTO?

A Data Transfer Object (DTO) is an object that carries data between layers or systems. It has no business logic no methods that do anything meaningful just fields representing the data being passed around.

The term was coined by Martin Fowler in Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture. The original purpose was to reduce the number of remote calls by batching data into one object. Today it's used more broadly to decouple internal domain models from external API contracts.

ANALOGY: A DELIVERY BOX

When a courier delivers a package, the box itself doesn't know what's inside or what to do with it. It just carries the items safely from sender to receiver. A DTO is that box a simple container that moves data from one layer to another without understanding or processing it.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780651751667-236827095.png
DTO (Data Transfer Object)

This diagram shows a DTO (Data Transfer Object) being used to transfer data from the User Service to the User Controller. The UserDTO contains only user-related data such as id, name, email, and createdAt. Its purpose is simply to carry data between different layers of the application.

The important point highlighted in the diagram is that a DTO contains data only and no business logic. It does not perform validations, calculations, or business operations. It acts as a lightweight container that helps exchange data cleanly and safely between components.
A DTO is a dumb data container. It knows nothing about the business. It just carries fields from A to B.
2. The Problem DTOs Solve
Without DTOs, you might expose your domain model (the internal entities) directly to the outside world the API, the database, other services. This creates three serious problems.
Problem 1: Leaking sensitive data

Your User entity has a passwordHash field, a createdAt timestamp, internal flags like isDeleted, and a role enum. If you return the raw entity in an API response, all of that leaks out to the client even the fields they were never meant to see.
RETURNING THE DOMAIN ENTITY DIRECTLY: LEAKS EVERYTHING
Problem 2: Tight coupling between API and database
blocks.text: Problem 2: Tight coupling between API and database

blocks.content: If your API response mirrors your database table exactly, changing the database schema (renaming a column, splitting a table) breaks the API contract immediately. Clients are now tightly coupled to your internals.
Problem 3: Accepting too much from clients
blocks.text: Problem 3: Accepting too much from clients

blocks.content: If you use the same object for both input and output, a malicious client could send fields they shouldn't be able to set like id, role, or createdAt.
CLIENT SENDS A USER OBJECT AND SETS THEIR OWN ROLE
DTO ONLY EXPOSES WHAT YOU WANT TO ACCEPT
ANALOGY: THE RESTAURANT MENU

A restaurant has a full inventory list in the kitchen every ingredient, cost price, supplier, expiry date. The menu the customer sees is a curated subset: dish name, description, price. The menu is a DTO. The inventory is the domain model. Customers never see the kitchen's internal list only what the restaurant chooses to expose.
3. DTO vs Domain Model

4. DTO Mapping
This diagram shows the process of converting an Entity into a DTO before sending data to the client.

The User Entity retrieved from the database contains everything related to the user, including public data, internal fields, sensitive information, and business logic. However, clients do not need access to all of this information.

Before sending the data in an API response, the application performs DTO Mapping, where only the required fields are copied from the Entity into a UserResponseDTO. In this example, the DTO contains only id, name, email, and createdAt.

The API then returns the DTO instead of the Entity. This ensures that internal details, sensitive data, and business logic remain hidden from clients while exposing only the information that should be publicly available.
In short:
Database → Entity (all data) → DTO Mapping → Response DTO (required data only) → API Response.
5. DTO in the Request-Response Flow
DTOs sit at the boundary of your system they're the first thing that receives incoming data and the last thing that goes out. Everything in the middle works with domain models.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1780651753071-591990019.png
Request DTOs and Response DTOs are used in a typical API request lifecycle.

When a client sends a request, it does not directly send data to the database or service layer. Instead, the request data is first captured in a Request DTO, which contains only the information needed from the client, such as name, email, and password.
The Controller receives this Request DTO and passes it to the Service layer. The service contains the business logic and interacts with the database to create, update, or retrieve data.

After the operation is completed, the service does not return the database entity directly. Instead, it creates a Response DTO containing only the fields that should be exposed to the client, such as id, name, email, and createdAt.
Finally, the controller converts the Response DTO into JSON and sends it back to the client.
The main idea is that:

["Request DTO defines what data the client can send.","Response DTO defines what data the client can receive.","Service contains the business logic.","Database entities stay hidden from the outside world."]
items: Request DTO defines what data the client can send.
Response DTO defines what data the client can receive.
Database entities stay hidden from the outside world.

blocks.content: Flow: Client → Request DTO → Controller → Service → Database → Response DTO → Client.

The key insight: domain models never cross the boundary. They stay inside the service layer. DTOs are created at the boundary converted from domain models on the way out, and converted to domain models on the way in.
6. Writing a DTO in Java
A DTO should be simple. Fields, constructor, getters. No business logic. Here's how to write them three different ways from verbose to modern.
Traditional class (Java 8+)
we'll use Java to implement DTOs because it is widely used in enterprise applications. However, the underlying concept is not specific to Java.
Whether you use C#, Go, Python, TypeScript, Kotlin, Rust, or any other language, the purpose and structure of a DTO remain the same. Only the syntax changes.
A DTO is simply a lightweight object used to transfer data between different layers of an application without containing business logic.
This means that while the examples below are written in Java, the same principles apply to DTOs in every programming language.

When sending the response back to the client, we do not expose the entire entity. A Response DTO is created containing only the fields that the client needs:
Fields such as passwordHash, role, internal flags, or other sensitive data are intentionally excluded.
That's why the flow is:
Raw Client Data → Request DTO → User Entity → Response DTO → Safe API Response
The Request DTO protects what can come into the system, while the Response DTO controls what can go out of the system.
8. Request DTO vs Response DTO
One of the most important decisions: should you use one DTO for both input and output, or separate DTOs? The answer is almost always: separate them.
1. Request DTO

A Request DTO represents the data sent by the client to the server. It contains only the fields that the client is allowed to provide as part of the request. Request DTOs are typically validated before being processed by the application and should not contain server-managed fields such as IDs, timestamps, or internal flags.
2. Response DTO

A Response DTO represents the data returned by the server to the client. It contains only the information that the client needs to see and should never expose sensitive data such as passwords or internal implementation details. Response DTOs are often designed to be immutable to ensure the returned data cannot be modified accidentally.
TIP: HAVE AS MANY DTOS AS YOU NEED

Don't be afraid of multiple DTOs. A "summary" DTO for list views, a "detail" DTO for single item views, a "create" DTO, an "update" DTO each tailored to its specific use case. Reusing one DTO for everything leads to either over-fetching or over-exposing.

9. Common Mistakes

DTOs are intentionally simple, but developers often misuse them by mixing responsibilities, exposing internal data, or treating them like domain objects, leading to tight coupling and maintainability issues.
Mistake 1: Putting business logic inside a DTO
blocks.text: Mistake 1: Putting business logic inside a DTO

blocks.content: A DTO that validates complex business rules, calculates totals, or makes decisions is no longer a DTO it's a service pretending to be a DTO. Keep business logic in the service layer.
BUSINESS LOGIC IN A DTO
Mistake 2: Using the domain entity as the DTO
blocks.text: Mistake 2: Using the domain entity as the DTO

blocks.content: Returning your JPA entity directly from a REST controller couples your API to your database schema and leaks internal fields. Every time you change the entity, the API changes. Every time you add a sensitive field to the entity, it might accidentally get exposed.
Mistake 3: One giant DTO for everything
blocks.text: Mistake 3: One giant DTO for everything

blocks.content: A UserDTO with 40 fields used for creation, update, listing, and detail views is a maintenance nightmare. Fields meant for one use case carry through all the others. Use purpose-specific DTOs they're cheap to create.
Mistake 4: Mutable response DTOs
If a response DTO has setters, any code that receives it could silently mutate the data before the response is sent. Response DTOs should be immutable use record or final fields with no setters.
Mistake 5: Skipping validation on request DTOs
blocks.text: Mistake 5: Skipping validation on request DTOs

blocks.content: A request DTO that accepts any value without validation means invalid data propagates deep into your service and domain layer before failing. Validate at the boundary the moment the DTO is created.
NO VALIDATION: BAD DATA REACHES THE SERVICE

items: A DTO is a simple data container fields only, no business logic, no behaviour. Its only job is to move data between layers or systems.
DTOs decouple your internal domain model from what you expose externally protecting sensitive fields, decoupling the API from the database schema, and controlling what clients can send.
Domain models stay inside the service layer. DTOs live at the boundary they're the first thing in (requests) and last thing out (responses).
Use separate DTOs for requests and responses they serve different purposes and have different fields.
Have as many DTOs as your use cases need summary, detail, create, update. Purpose-specific DTOs are cheap and clear.
Response DTOs should be immutable. Request DTOs should validate their input at construction time.
Use Java record for DTOs immutable, auto-generated equals/hashCode/toString, zero boilerplate.
Map between DTOs and domain models in a dedicated mapper class or using MapStruct keep the mapping logic out of controllers and services.
Never put business logic inside a DTO. If it's calculating, deciding, or validating domain rules it belongs in the service layer.
